Access host

  • While you can manage most aspects of the OCP through the UI, there are tasks you will need to perform using either kubectl or the OpenShift Client (oc). If you only wish to use one client, oc adds specific OpenShift features which kubectl does not have access to. You can run the utilities on Windows or Linux or even MacOS.

    In the RedHat Hybrid Cloud Console, navigate to Resources -> Download in Figure 35.

    Figure 35.    OC download

    Simply copy over the Kube configuration from the cluster to your VM or server that has network access to the cluster. We used a SUSE 15.6 VM here, but any OS distribution is acceptable, including using AMD. It’s advisable to set up the host prior to deployment because it is useful for the public key creation that allows SSH access to the hosts after installation.

    OpenShift node access

    One of the peculiarities of an OpenShift implementation as detailed here is that you cannot simply SSH into a node as root or another user like you would in other Kubernetes clusters. OCP locks down that type of access which is why it is essential to set up an SSH public key you can supply to the installer. If you keep this key on your access host, it will permit you to SSH into the nodes as the “core” user and then run commands as sudo. There are situations that will require you to do this, particularly if there are networking problems you must diagnose. To create this key, you can follow these simple steps:

    [root@dsib0111 ~]# ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "dell-user@dell.com"

    Generating public/private rsa key pair.

    Enter file in which to save the key (/root/.ssh/id_rsa):

    Enter passphrase for "/root/.ssh/id_rsa" (empty for no passphrase):

    Enter same passphrase again:

    Your identification has been saved in /root/.ssh/id_rsa

    Your public key has been saved in /root/.ssh/id_rsa.pub

    The key fingerprint is:

    SHA256:n3jair3L/5WG3TPLuMO/xRk1yuaDg4QE+ezddO/Djio dell-user@dell.com

    The key's randomart image is:

    +---[RSA 4096]----+

    |     ..          |

    |     ..          |

    |      o.       ..|

    |      .o.  .... o|

    |      ..S.o .+.. |

    |       ..+.o+o =o|

    |        ..+oooB++|

    |       + E  .==+=|

    |      . B=+oo+=*o|

    +----[SHA256]-----+

    [root@dsib0111 ~]#

    You will supply the file /root/.ssh/id_rsa.pub to the installer at the appropriate step. You will then be able to ssh into the OCP nodes:

    ospmax170:~/.kube # ssh core@ospmax151.openshift.pmax.com

    Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS 9.6.20250930-0

      Part of OpenShift 4.19, RHCOS is a Kubernetes-native operating system

      managed by the Machine Config Operator (`clusteroperator/machine-config`).

    WARNING: Direct SSH access to machines is not recommended; instead,

    make configuration changes via `machineconfig` objects:

      https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.19/architecture/architecture-rhcos.html

    ---

    Last login: Fri Oct 24 13:45:24 2025 from 172.16.105.170

    [systemd]

    Failed Units: 1

      NetworkManager-wait-online.service

    [core@ospmax151 ~]$

Assisted Installer

  • The Assisted Installer is one of the solutions available to install OCP. Red Hat offers it as SaaS through the Red Hat Hybrid Cloud Console, and it is the recommended methodology as it reduces the complexity inherent in some of the other solutions. The installer focuses on various solutions including bare metal, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, vSphere, and Nutanix. In this paper’s on-premises implementation, the Installer supports the following different options:

    • Highly available OpenShift Container Platform or single-node OpenShift cluster
    • OpenShift Container Platform on bare metal or vSphere with full platform integration, or other virtualization platforms without integration
    • OpenShift Virtualization and Red Hat OpenShift Data Foundation

    Click Create cluster to start the process.

    Figure 6.   Creating a new cluster through Red Hat Hybrid Cloud Console

    Navigate to the Datacenter tab and click on Create cluster again.

    Figure 7.   Datacenter create cluster

    Note: The gray menu on the left-hand side in Figure 7 does not change throughout the Assisted Installer. Therefore, to enhance image quality, we removed them from the installation wizard images in this paper. We similarly removed the feedback and chat icons when required.

    Step 1 Cluster details

    In the first step, most of the values are default. Enter a Cluster name and Base domain (note the DNS entry requirement) and select the Hosts’ network configuration, DHCP or Static IP at the bottom of the screen. If you desire encryption, toggle one or more of the entries. The OpenShift version will always default to the most current version available. If necessary, adjust it to meet the support requirements of integrated components such as the PowerMax CSI driver. Click Next.

     

    Figure 8.   Step 1 – Cluster creation

    Step 2a Static network configurations: Network-wide configurations

    If you selected static IP in step 1, as in this wizard, step 2 covers both network-wide and host specific settings. If you selected DHCP, there is no network step at all, and the total steps reduce to six from seven.

    For static IP, in the first screen the Configure via setting defaults to the Form view and is appropriate for most clusters. Choose the Networking stack type, a VLAN if desired, and the IP information. Click Next to move to host specific settings.

    Figure 9.   Step 2a – Cluster creation

    Step 2b Static network configurations: Host specific configurations

    The second part of step 2 requires that you obtain the MAC addresses of the NIC or NICs on the designated host. As these are Dell servers, we obtained the addresses using iDRAC. Below is an example of port one of the first NIC. This solution uses two NICs.

    Figure 10.    MAC address from iDRAC

    Once you have the MAC address(es), enter the information into the wizard. As we are using two NIC ports, we check the Use bond box with the recommended Bond type of Active-Backup.

    Figure 11.    Step 2b – Cluster creation

    As you add each host, the previous host(s) show at the top as in Figure 12. Complete the process for all three hosts, or however many hosts there are in your cluster.

     

    Figure 12.    Step 2b – Cluster creation

    Step 3 Operators

    In this step you choose the Operators, which have bundles of software that enable specific features. We want to run both containerized applications and VMs in this cluster, so we check the Virtualization bundle. There are 26 Single Operators that you may choose from. Expand the list to check individual Operators such as Logical Volume Manager Storage. Checking the Virtualization bundle activates twelve required Operators. Click Next.

     

    Figure 13.    Step 3 – Cluster creation

    Step 4 Host discovery

    The Assisted Installer discovers hosts through a discovery ISO. You mount this ISO on each of your OpenShift bare metal hosts, and it boots to a temporary Red Hat OS. The Installer queries for the hosts by the IP address you supply in Figure 11. Begin by clicking the Add hosts button under Host discovery. This will start another wizard that guides you to download the Discovery ISO.

     

    Figure 14.    Step 4 – Cluster creation

    In the first dialog, select a Provisioning type. It defaults to Minimal image file which Dell recommends. It is about 130 MB in size. Supply an SSH public key as detailed in OpenShift node access.

    The dialog also offers settings for proxy and certificates if appropriate for your environment. Click Generate Discovery ISO in Figure 15.

     

    Figure 15.    Step 4a – Cluster creation

    The creation of the ISO is a quick process. The installer presents a second dialog so that you can download the ISO either through the browser or wget. Choose a method and download the ISO to a location that has access to the management interface of the OpenShift nodes, e.g., iDRAC.

     

    Figure 16.    Step 4b – Cluster creation

    Next, mount the ISO to the designated nodes, and reboot to the ISO. In this cluster there are three bare-metal machines. Below is an example of the first node in this cluster. Note the new bond, bond0 on VLAN 105, with the correct IP in Figure 17 after the initial configuration completes. At this point, the installer will be able to discover the node.

    Figure 17.    Step 4c – Cluster creation

    Be sure all nodes reach this point after booting to the ISO. The installer takes a few minutes to recognize the nodes, but when it does, they will appear in the wizard. Wait for the Status to show Ready in Figure 18. As the installer discovers the hosts, it may display other statuses such as Not Ready until it finishes the initial configuration. If the installer detects an issue, the status will remain as something other than Ready at which time you should troubleshoot using the OCP documentation found in the References. It is also possible for the installer to show Ready but also include warnings. Click Next.

    Figure 18.    Step 4d – Cluster creation

    Step 5 Storage

    • In the storage step it is usually unnecessary to make any modifications because the installer will use the internal disk if it meets the size requirements. The OpenShift Container Platform
    • OpenShift Virtualization - Reference Implementation Guide
    • Offload README

    Appendix covers the use case where external disks exist. The installer warns the user that it will format all bootable disks. If you wish to review the inventory before proceeding, use the greater than symbol (>) to expand each server. Click Next.

    Figure 19.    Step 5 – Cluster creation

    Step 6 Networking

    In the Networking page you must decide whether you or the cluster will manage the network. Dell recommends the Cluster-Managed Networking for most implementations. The Network stack type defaults but choose a Machine network from the drop-down menu. You will need two additional IPs for the API and Ingress. If needed, there are advanced networking capabilities you can explore by checking the box.

    The bottom half of Figure 20 includes the discovered hosts. The installer runs a few preliminary checks on them, specifically a test for clock synchronization. If this fails, as below, the installer grays out the Next button. You can see the Status of one of the hosts is Insufficient because its clock is too far askew from the other two.

    Figure 20.    Step 6 – Cluster creation

    To resolve this error, you need to manually add an NTP server. You can do this by clicking the hyperlink below the Ready status where it says Some validations failed. A pop-up shows you that there is no NTP server. Click Add NTP sources in Figure 21 and enter the IP address. Click Add. You only need to do this once on any of the hosts as the NTP server is then set on all of the nodes in the cluster.

     

    Figure 21.    Step 6a – Cluster creation

    After you add the NTP server, it will take a few minutes for all hosts to synchronize with the NTP. Eventually the installer will remove the validation error, and all hosts will enter Ready status. Note that the yellow box error at the bottom may remain a bit longer while the clock on that insufficient host synchronizes; but until it disappears you will be unable to click Next.

    Figure 22.    Step 6b – Cluster creation

    Step 7 Review and create

    In the last step, the installer runs a number of pre-checks to ensure the installation is likely to succeed. You can review the summary of each major section before clicking Install cluster. Once you do that, a small notice appears to the right indicating the start and the Install cluster button turns gray. The image below only includes a couple of the summary sections for brevity.

    Figure 23.    Step 7 – Cluster creation

    You can watch the installation progress in the Hybrid Cloud Console. When it completes, it will show the host inventory in Figure 24, and you can launch the OpenShift Web Console.

    Note: You will need to be sure that the DNS has the necessary entries to access the console URL, or alternatively that you add the names to the local hosts file on the bastion server. Click on the Not able to access the Web Console hyperlink to get a list of the required entries. You can find an example of the DNS entries in the Appendix section DNS entries.

     

    Figure 24.    Cluster installation completion

    If it becomes necessary to scale the OCP cluster, you can expand it in much the same manner as the original installation. The next section covers this.

Containerized applications

  • You can deploy applications on OCP using the web console or CLI. The UI offers a software catalog of common applications, services, and templates. Since many of these catalog items use a DeploymentConfig rather than a Deployment, be aware that Red Hat deprecated the DeploymentConfig object in OpenShift version 4.14.

    Figure 54.    DeploymentConfig deprecation

    Because Red Hat continues to publish the catalog items, the next section will demonstrate both a deploymentconfig and deployment of the same database, MySQL.

    DeploymentConfig

    Create a MySQL deploymentconfig by following these steps.

    Step 1

    Login to the web console and navigate in the UI to Home -> Software Catalog in the left-hand menu. In the right-hand panel select All items -> Databases -> MySQL. Click on the first template which requires persistent storage.

    Figure 55.    Step 1 – MySQL deploymentconfig

    Step 2

    Next click on Instantiate Template to open the entry form.

    Figure 56.    Step 2 – MySQL deploymentconfig

    Step 3

    The template does not require any changes if you are taking the defaults. In this example below, however, we adjusted the namespace to mysql and updated the volume capacity from 1 to 10 Gi. Since this template uses persistent storage, it is essential you have a default storage class for the Dell PowerMax. Click Create to complete the template and deploy MySQL.

    Figure 57.    Step 3 – MySQL deploymentconfig

    You can access the new deployment through the left-hand menu Workloads -> DeploymentConfigs and then in the right-hand panel select your project. The UI offers direct access to the MySQL pod through a terminal, if desired.

    Figure 58.    MySQL deploymentconfig

    Here you can see the PowerMax 10 GB persistent storage for the pod, using the default storage class powermax-fc-sc.

    Figure 59.    PowerMax persistent storage for MySQL deploymentconfig

    Deployment

    Unlike the deploymentconfig which creates all objects as part of the template, a deployment of the same MySQL database entails creating the storage, deployment, and service separately. Create a MySQL deployment by following these steps.

    Step 1

    Login to the web console and navigate in the UI to Storage -> PersistentVolumeClaims in the left-hand menu. In the right-hand panel click Create PersistentVolumeClaim. In the YAML form enter in the required information. Note here we are using the storage class  powermax-bronze-fc since this is a test environment and does not require high performance. Click Create to complete.

    Figure 60.    Step 1 – MySQL deployment

    Step 2

    Next navigate to Workloads -> Deployment in the left-hand menu. In the right-hand panel click Create Deployment. In the Create Deployment wizard, choose the view, Form or YAML, and enter the required information. Be sure to reference the PVC you created in step 1. Click Create to complete.

    Figure 61.    Step 2 – MySQL deployment

    Step 3

    Finally, create the service. Navigate to Network -> Services. In the right-hand panel click Create Service. Enter the required information and click Create.

    Figure 62.    Step 3 – MySQL deployment

    The new deployment is complete.

    Figure 63.    MySQL deployment

Document purpose

  • This guide provides configuration details for deploying Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform on Dell servers, leveraging Dell PowerMax (PowerMax) for persistent storage. It covers the setup of a bare-metal cluster utilizing Red Hat’s Assisted Installer and includes examples of deploying both a containerized application and a virtual machine on that cluster. Additionally, it demonstrates how to migrate virtual machines from VMware to OpenShift and highlights a Red Hat technology option that offloads the copy process, significantly decreasing the time to migrate.

    Note: The contents of this document are valid for the software and hardware versions described. For information about updated configurations for newer software and hardware versions, contact your Red Hat or Dell Technologies sales representative.

External networks

  • If you need to access a virtual machine (VM) from outside the OpenShift cluster, you have several options with varying complexity. The most effective approach is to use an additional NIC on the OpenShift node for VM traffic. To do this, identify the extra physical interface, ensure it is active, and confirm it is available. Then create a NetworkAttachmentDefinition (using Multus) that references this interface, typically through a bridged connection. Alternatively, you can create a secondary Open vSwitch (OVS) bridge bound to the NIC. When you define the VM or pod, attach it to this network so it can obtain an IP address from your physical network via DHCP or static assignment. Verify that firewalls, VLANs, and network policies allow the intended traffic. This configuration isolates VM traffic on the extra NIC while keeping OpenShift management and default pod networks separate.

    Note: Red Hat does not recommend utilizing the cluster network devices for external access.

    This procedure executes commands directly on the OCP nodes. Red Hat recommends using a MachineConfig file rather than accessing the nodes. If you prefer that model, there is an example in the Adding a VM bridged network section of the Appendix.

    Adding a bridged network

    To create the bridge and slave, ssh into your node as the “core” user from a box configured for this purpose. In this simple example, I am using one NIC, eno3, which is up and not part of the OpenShift environment. The names of the bridge and slave are arbitrary.

    Step 1

    Delete any existing profiles for the NIC in question. In this example I am using eno3.

    sudo nmcli connection delete br-eno3

    sudo nmcli connection delete bridge-slave-eno3

    Step 2

    Create the bridge. Since we intend this network for use by the VMs, we do not assign an IP to it.

    sudo nmcli connection add type bridge ifname br-eno3 con-name br-eno3 ipv4.method disabled ipv6.method ignore

    Step 3

    Add eno3 as the slave to the master bridge.

    sudo nmcli connection add type ethernet ifname eno3 con-name bridge-slave-eno3 master br-eno3

    Step 4

    Finally set the interfaces to auto-connect on reboot and bring them up.

    sudo nmcli connection modify br-eno3 connection.autoconnect yes

    sudo nmcli connection modify bridge-slave-eno3 connection.autoconnect yes

    sudo nmcli connection up br-eno3

    sudo nmcli connection up bridge-slave-eno3

    Once complete, exit the session.

    VM network

    To enable the VM to use the new network, use Multus to configure a NetworkAttachmentDefinition (NAD). Multus is a CNI plugin for Kubernetes that enables attaching multiple network interfaces to pods. By default, Kubernetes only supports one network interface per pod. A NetworkAttachmentDefinition (NAD) is a Kubernetes custom resource (CRD) that defines how a pod should connect to an additional network.

    In this environment, we created the following NAD which permits assigning the network to multiple VMs.

    apiVersion: k8s.cni.cncf.io/v1

    kind: NetworkAttachmentDefinition

    metadata:

      name: br-eno3-network

      namespace: production-vms

      annotations:

        kubevirt.io/network-binding: bridge

        k8s.v1.cni.cncf.io/resourceName: bridge.network.kubevirt.io/br-eno3

    spec:

      config: |

        {

          "cniVersion": "0.3.1",

          "type": "bridge",

          "bridge": "br-eno3",

          "isGateway": true

        }

    When you create a VM or attach a network adapter to an existing one, you can specify the bridged network as in Figure 53.

    Figure 53.    Adding bridged network to VM

Introduction

  • The following sections detail the creation of VMs and containers on the OCP platform. OCP offers the ability to run both virtual machines and containerized applications on the same platform. When you deploy VMs on OCP, however, you are still using Kubernetes objects like pods and persistent volumes as the foundation. This is distinct from other hypervisors in which you deploy many VMs to a single storage volume with a file system, e.g., VMFS.

Migration Toolkit for Virtualization

  • The Migration Toolkit for Virtualization, or MTV, provides a comprehensive solution for moving existing virtual machines from platforms such as VMware vSphere, Red Hat Virtualization and OpenStack into a modern container-based environment powered by Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization. It enables the planning, migration, and management of VM workloads to run natively within OpenShift, helping organizations accelerate cloud-native adoption, reduce operational complexity, and modernize infrastructure. By supporting cold, warm, and live migration workflows, and by providing mapping tools for storage, network and compute resources, the toolkit offers flexibility for on-premises and hybrid cloud scenarios.

    MTV is an installed Operator. It supports a number of providers from which you can migrate in Figure 64. There are three modes of migration:

    • Cold – Powered off VMs. It does not require common storage. It supports all providers.
    • Warm – Powered on VMs. It does not require common storage but only supports VMware vSphere and Red Hat Virtualization providers.
    • Live – Powered on VMs. It requires common storage, and it only supports OpenShift Virtualization clusters or migration within the same cluster across namespaces.

    Figure 64.    Migration Toolkit for Virtualization

    For cold and warm modes, MTV performs network-based migrations, transferring virtual machine data and configurations from the source hypervisor to OpenShift Virtualization over the network. MTV copies disk images and metadata through managed data transfer channels, ensuring that it recreates virtual machines accurately in the target OpenShift cluster.

OCP environment

  • The following is information about the specific environment detailed in this paper.

    Cluster

    This paper describes the deployment of a three-node, bare metal Red Hat OpenShift cluster running version 4.19.15. The update channel is stable-4.19.

    Network topology

    For the environment in this paper the following network exists. At the physical layer, there are two Top of Rack (TOR) switches used for redundancy and load-balancing purposes. There are two connections from each Dell host NIC used in the solution, one to TOR A and one to TOR B.

    Each OCP host has two, two-port HBAs (32 Gb min) with connectivity to the PowerMax array. We zoned each HBA port to an FA port on the array so that a single HBA connects to two different directors as in Figure 4 (switches are implied). For larger arrays with more directors, spread connectivity over multiple engines.

    Dell PowerMax storage

    In an OpenShift cluster, array storage like Dell PowerMax provides persistent, high-performance, and reliable storage for VMs and containerized applications. Unlike ephemeral storage tied to individual nodes, array storage ensures data survives pod restarts, node failures, and scaling operations. It enables features like dynamic volume provisioning, persistent volumes, and storage classes, allowing applications to access shared storage efficiently. This is critical for stateful workloads such as databases, message queues, and enterprise applications that require consistent data availability and performance across the cluster.

    Dell PowerMax arrays provide tiered performance through service levels, which you can map to storage classes. This allows you to assign the appropriate service level to each VM or container for optimal performance.

    Service levels

    A service level is a property of a storage group, a provisioning object on Dell PowerMax. The service level defines the maximum and minimum response times for I/O operations that involve the storage group. The minimum response time (known as the floor) defines the shortest time that each I/O operation on the storage group takes to complete. The maximum response time (known as the ceiling) defines the longest, acceptable time for any I/O operation on the storage group. PowerMax uses the floor and ceiling values to monitor whether each storage group complies with its quality-of-service criteria.

    The storage administrator can use the service levels to help ensure that lower-priority applications do not impede storage groups associated with high-priority applications. The six service levels on the PowerMax are the following, beginning with the highest priority, and shown in Figure 5:

    • Diamond
    • Platinum
    • Gold
    • Silver
    • Bronze
    • Optimized

    Figure 5.   PowerMax service levels

    Under normal operating conditions, PowerMax ensures that the performance is commensurate with the chosen service level’s compliance range. If, however, there is contention, PowerMax will prioritize higher service levels by limiting performance of the lower service levels. Therefore, it is essential to select the storage class best suited for the performance needs of the VM disk or containerized application.

Offload option

  • The Migration Toolkit for Virtualization includes an offload option that significantly decreases VM migration time in comparison to using the VDDK.

    Prerequisites

    PowerMax offload requires the following prerequisites. Note that these are valid as of the publication of the paper and may change in the future. Always refer to the Red Hat documentation for the most up-to-date information.

    • MTV 2.11.0 or higher
    • VMware vSphere as the source of the virtual machine
    • The vmkfstools-wrapper VIB (installed automatically by default)
    • XCOPY must be disabled on the ESXi host unless you patch the HYPERMAX OS/PowerMaxOS. See the XCOPY section below.

    Offload process

    MTV conducts virtual machines migrations across the IP network, from a source hypervisor to OCP. Depending on the speed of the network and the amount of data to transfer, this can be a time-consuming task. Red Hat determined that, on VMware vSphere, if they could move the copy to the ESXi host, it would reduce the time to complete a migration significantly. They accomplish this with the ESXi utility vmkfstools.

    Excluding VM creation tasks, as an example, the offload workflow for a cold migration consists of:

    • Create the target device using the storage class specified in the migration plan.
    • Mask the target device to the ESXi host where the VM resides using the port group specified in the secret. MTV generates unique auto provisioning objects on PowerMax for the initiator and storage groups, and the masking view.
    • Run a vmkfstools clone – this can be a vmdk to RDM or RDM to RDM.
    • Unmask the target device from the ESXi host.
    • Mask the device to OCP.

    OpenShift only powers down the source VM if necessary before a cold migration. It does not delete the VMware source VM after the migration completes.

    Figure 77.    Offload workflow

    Note: Warm migrations will use network copy for any changes that occur to the source VM during and after the offload process. This utilizes change block tracking (CBT) on VMware. OpenShift copies on an hourly interval. To avoid excess network copy with offload, Dell recommends cutting over soon after the offload completes.

    The offload feature is an option of the storage mapping portion of the migration plan. There are three values you set by drop-down:

    • Offload plugin – There is only one option, vSphere XCOPY. Note that this is simply the name of the plug-in and does not mean it requires XCOPY to work.
    • Storage secret – A secret which has both generic and specific values for the storage product.
    • Storage product – The storage array to use in offload.

    Figure 78.    Offload options

    vmkfstools-wrapper

    The offload uses a custom VIB (vSphere Installation Bundle) installed on ESXi hosts to expose vmkfstools operations via the vSphere API. The first migration plan you run on an ESXi host will place the vmkfstools-wrapper.vib file in the first VM’s VMFS datastore’s top directory. It will install the VIB and it will remain installed for future migrations. There is no manual intervention unless you wish to uninstall it after testing. Once installed, the VIB appears as below.

    [root@dsib1040:~] esxcli software vib list |grep RED

    vmkfstools-wrapper 0.1.1 REDHAT  CommunitySupported 

    If you prefer a different, manual solution around the use of the VIB, please see the README in the Red Hat documentation section and search for SSH.

    XCOPY

    The plugin name can be misleading because the offload process does not use XCOPY; it shifts from a network-based copy to using vmkfstools on the ESXi host. If the storage array supports the XCOPY primitive, vmkfstools calls XCOPY during migration because VMware designed it that way. This happens whether MTV runs vmkfstools or the user runs it manually—it’s a vSphere feature. Some arrays, such as Dell PowerFlex, do not support XCOPY, yet the offload still works correctly on those platforms.

    While PowerMax supports XCOPY, vmkfstools cannot use it in any release of HYPERMAX OS or PowerMaxOS through version 10.3.0 without an ePack. The following are the necessary ePacks:

    • PowerMaxOS 10.3.1.0 - ePack is the Q126 (11248)
    • HYPERMAX OS 5978.720.720 - ePack is the Q126 (11249)

    If you apply one of these ePacks, you can leave XCOPY enabled (default). If you do not apply the ePack or you are at a version without one, you must disable XCOPY on the ESXi host before you migrate. If you do not, and you issue a vmkfstools clone either manually or as part of a migration offload when XCOPY is enabled, the command will fail with a timeout. For an offload migration, the error will be in the populate-xx log:

    I1110 14:01:46.113237       1 vsphere-xcopy-volume-populator.go:219] channel quit clone task failed with exit code 255, stderr: Failed to clone disk: Connection timed out (7208969).

    F1110 14:01:46.113274       1 vsphere-xcopy-volume-populator.go:221] clone task failed with exit code 255, stderr: Failed to clone disk: Connection timed out (7208969).

    Therefore, it is essential to disable XCOPY on the ESXi host prior to running an offload migration if you do not have the ePack. You can disable it in the UI or CLI. The UI location is in Advanced System Settings of the ESXi host. Set the value to ‘0’ to disable.

    Figure 79.    Disabling XCOPY in the UI

    For the CLI, login to the ESXi host and issue:

    esxcfg-advcfg -s 0 /DataMover/HardwareAcceleratedMove

    After you finish migration testing you can re-enable XCOPY.

    Storage secret

    One of the offload options is the selection of a storage secret. This secret for PowerMax must have the fields in Table 4.

    Table 4.      PowerMax storage secret for offload

    Key

    Description

    STORAGE_HOSTNAME

    URL of Unisphere for PowerMax, including port

    STORAGE_USERNAME

    Username of Unisphere for PowerMax

    STORAGE_PASSWORD

    Password of Unisphere for PowerMax

    STORAGE_SKIP_SSL_VERIFICATION

    Certificate verification (default is FALSE)

    POWERMAX_SYMMETRIX_ID

    PowerMax array ID as used by the CSI driver

    POWERMAX_PORT_GROUP_NAME

    PowerMax FC port group name that contains the zoned ports of the ESXi migration host

    All these fields are mandatory except STORAGE_SKIP_SSL_VERIFICATION, but it defaults to false. You can take the values from your PowerMax CSI driver setup. One of the secrets in this setup is below:

    apiVersion: v1

    kind: Secret

    metadata:

      name: powermax-1473-storage-secret

      namespace: openshift-mtv

    type: Opaque

    stringData:

      STORAGE_HOSTNAME: "https://172.16.105.200:8443"

      STORAGE_USERNAME: "smc"

      STORAGE_PASSWORD: "smc"

      POWERMAX_SYMMETRIX_ID: "000120001473"

      POWERMAX_PORT_GROUP_NAME: "mtv_group_pg"

    Create this secret prior to configuring a migration plan.

    Network and offload performance

    VM migration over the network can take significantly longer than using the offload feature. Network speed is a critical factor for network-based migration, but it does not affect offload performance.

    The following results compare two migration methods—network-based and offload—for the same VM. This VM contains a single, fully populated 100 GB VMDK. The first image shows the network migration, and the second shows the offload migration.

    Figure 80.    Network migration of dsib2122.drm.lab.emc.com

    Figure 81.    Offload migration of dsib2122.drm.lab.emc.com

    Note: Unlike a network copy, the offload feature does not show Disk transfer progress in the UI. The amount copied will remain at zero until completion, at which time it will update to the disk size.

    The network migration took 24 minutes to transfer 100 GB, while the offload completed in just 2 minutes—a 10× improvement. Faster IP infrastructure can reduce network migration time, but it will always be significantly slower than offload.

    Different PowerMax source and target

    Offload will work between two different PowerMax arrays by meeting the following conditions:

    • Target and source arrays configured in the CSI driver.
    • Migration ESXi host has access to both arrays through host groups.
    • A secret exists for the target array with the correct port group name.
    • There is an available storage class for the target array.

    Raw Device Mappings (RDM)

    RDMs with MTV and offload is an interesting use case because MTV does not support RDMs when using network copy. You can see below the “Critical concerns” you get for the VM, clearly pointing out the restriction.

    Figure 82.    RDM critical concern

    When you use offload, however, you are not doing a network copy but a vmkfstools clone. A vmkfstools clone supports RDMs, therefore offloading works with RDMs. When you configure the VM in the migration plan, however, you must acknowledge the restriction:

    Figure 83.    Confirm selections despite RDM

    After confirming, the migration plan proceeds as any non-RDM plan.

    Note: The offload supports VMware virtual volumes (vVols).

Overview

  • OpenShift Container Platform (OCP) is a robust, cloud-based solution built on Kubernetes and designed to support the development, deployment, and management of containerized applications at scale. Leveraging Kubernetes as its core, OpenShift extends its capabilities to enable seamless scalability from small environments to large, enterprise-grade infrastructures serving millions of users.

    Key benefits of OpenShift Container Platform include:

    • Developer and IT Enablement: Offers a secure, scalable cloud application platform that simplifies deployment and accelerates development cycles.
    • Operational Efficiency: Minimizes configuration and management overhead, streamlining operations for IT teams.
    • Hybrid Cloud Flexibility: Brings Kubernetes to both on-premises data centers and public cloud environments, supporting diverse infrastructure strategies.
    • Enterprise-Grade Compliance: Meets stringent requirements for security, privacy, compliance, and governance, making it suitable for regulated industries.

    To deliver persistent storage for demanding workloads, this solution integrates Dell PowerMax, providing exceptional performance, scalability, and advanced data services such as replication for backup and disaster recovery. Together, OpenShift and PowerMax empower organizations to modernize their application infrastructure while maintaining control, security, and agility across environments.

Persistent volumes

  • A Persistent Volume (PV) represents a storage resource that you provision for use within a cluster. It abstracts the underlying storage system, allowing workloads to consume storage without managing implementation details. Unlike ephemeral volumes, a PV remains available after you delete pods, ensuring data persists across pod lifecycles. In this solution, Dell PowerMax serves as the persistent storage backend, delivering enterprise-grade performance and reliability for PVs.

    StorageClass

    A StorageClass defines the parameters and provisioner that Kubernetes uses to create PVs dynamically. When you create a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) and specify a StorageClass, Kubernetes provisions a PV that matches the class’s configuration—such as disk type, replication policy, or with Dell PowerMax, service level. By leveraging a StorageClass configured for Dell PowerMax, Kubernetes can automatically allocate high-performance, fault-tolerant storage resources, enabling dynamic, policy-driven storage allocation, and decoupling application requirements from physical infrastructure.

    When you create an OpenShift Container Platform (OCP) cluster, the installer adds a storage class called localblock-sc for local block storage. The installer uses this class during deployment, but it does not set it as the default. Some resources—such as virtual machine OS distribution boot volumes—require a default storage class before the cluster can create them automatically. To meet this requirement, create a default storage class backed by Dell PowerMax.

    You can create a default storage class through the CLI (oc or kubectl) or use the cluster console. We cover both below.

    OpenShift Web Console

    Step 1

    Navigate to Storage -> StorageClasses in the left-hand menu. In the right-hand panel click on Create StorageClass. Only the installer-created storage class will be present. 

    Figure 41.    Step 1 – Default storage class

    Step 2

    Provide the necessary details for the storage class. Use the drop-down menu for the Provisioner to select csi-powermax.dellemc.com. You will have to add two parameters. One is for the PowerMax ID, SYMID, and the other is for the SRP. If you fail to include these, provisioning will fail. Optionally, you can add ServiceLevel. Leave the check box selected for expansion and click Create.

    Figure 42.    Step 2 – Default storage class

    Step 3

    To set the class as default, you must edit the storage class after creation. Click on the three buttons next to the new storage class and select Set as default.

    Figure 43.    Step 3 – Default storage class

    The storage class will now be set as default in Figure 44.

    Figure 44.    Complete – Default storage class

    After you configure the default class, OpenShift provisions the boot volumes shown in the catalog and makes them available as templates for cloning when you deploy virtual machines.

    Note: Do not create more than one default storage class. It can lead to undesirable results.

    Figure 45.    Linux OS boot volumes with PowerMax volumes

    CLI via oc

    If you prefer to use CLI, kubectl or oc, you can specify greater detail in the YAML file. For example, knowing OpenShift uses this storage class for Linux OS boot volumes, you may wish to set the service level from the default of Diamond to something less performant such as Bronze. To do this, construct the following YAML as follows, the creation output is in Figure 46.

    apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1

    kind: StorageClass

    metadata:

      name: powermax-fc-sc

      annotations:

        storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"

    parameters:

      SRP: SRP_1

      SYMID: "000120001672"

      ServiceLevel: Bronze

      csi.storage.k8s.io/fstype: xfs

    provisioner: csi-powermax.dellemc.com

    reclaimPolicy: Delete

    volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer

    allowVolumeExpansion: true

    Figure 46.    Storage class via YAML

PowerMax

  • The PowerMax family represents the flagship products of the Dell Technologies enterprise storage business. It is a multi-node, active/active scale-out architecture using industry standard, end-to-end NVMe components. The platform features inline, global deduplication and compression, providing customers with high storage efficiency even as the system scales. The PowerMax family also provides what many consider to be the gold standard in data services, proven high availability and resiliency, and advanced security that adheres to stringent government regulations and corporate compliance requirements, such as FIPS 140-2 and FIPS 140-3. A core strength of the PowerMax family is its ability to consolidate workloads. One can use a single PowerMax system to consolidate from one-to-many types of workloads, and both block and file storage services.

    PowerMax systems are modular, enabling them to expand to meet the future needs of the customer. The PowerMax family of arrays has four models:

    • PowerMax 2500 with a maximum capacity of 8 PBe (Petabytes effective)
    • PowerMax 2000 with a maximum capacity of 1.2 PBe
    • PowerMax 8500 with a maximum capacity of 18 PBe
    • PowerMax 8000 with a maximum capacity of 4.5 PBe

    Dell configures the PowerMax at the factory with a single Storage Resource Pool, or SRP, which is comprised of the physical disks in the array, managed as data pools. The array uses this collection of data pools for capacity and performance management. All host devices are part of an SRP.

    PowerMax for Open Systems provides support for the following protocols:

    • Fiber-Channel (FC) and NVMe over FC (NVMe/FC) with speeds of 8 Gb/s, 16 Gb/s, or 32 Gb/s
    • iSCSI and NVMe over TCP (NVMe/TCP) with speed of 10 Gb/s or 25 Gb/s
    • SRDF over FC with speed of 8 Gb/s, 16 Gb/s, or 32 Gb/s
    • SRDF over IP with speed of 10 Gb/s or 25 Gb/s

    PowerMaxOS operating system

    PowerMaxOS is the advanced operating system that powers Dell PowerMax storage arrays, delivering a software-defined, performance-optimized platform designed for mission-critical enterprise workloads. It is a modern architecture that is modular, container-based, and tightly integrated with end-to-end NVMe hardware to offer ultra-low latency, high throughput, and automated efficiency.

    Built with intelligent machine learning, PowerMaxOS dynamically analyzes I/O patterns to optimize data placement and resource usage in real time. It supports inline compression and de-duplication, ensuring space efficiency. With native encryption, secure snapshots, and multi-tenancy features, PowerMaxOS also ensures strong data protection and isolation.

    PowerMax replication

    PowerMax local replication includes TimeFinder/SnapVX (snapshots) and TimeFinder/Clone (clones), while PowerMax remote replication includes the SRDF product line. TimeFinder provides point-in-time local replication and data protection, and SRDF provides continuous remote replication, high availability, and disaster recovery.

    You can initiate or restore PowerMax TimeFinder snapshots or clones on SRDF target devices. One benefit of this integration is that it allows the creation of remote copies of the source application without interrupting remote replication. If the source application data is corrupted, the remote snapshot (or clone) and SRDF can restore the data in parallel to the source volumes. SRDF sends only changed data during normal operation and utilizes write folding to reduce the network impact.

PowerMax CSI

  • The Container Storage Interface, or CSI, is an industry standard for exposing block and file storage to containerized applications like Kubernetes, a Container Orchestration System. The CSI drivers implement an interface between CSI-enabled Container Orchestrator (CO) and storage arrays. It is a plug-in you install into Kubernetes to provide persistent storage using a Dell storage system like PowerMax. The PowerMax CSI driver supports most protocols, capabilities, and access modes. Please see the Dell documentation here for details.

    Container Storage Modules enhance the CSI to provide advanced enterprise storage features for Kubernetes clusters. It includes software modules that extend beyond CSI, offering enterprise storage capabilities to Kubernetes users. These modules are Authorization, Replication, Snapshotting, Resiliency and Observability.

    The CSI driver installation instructions vary depending on the underlying Kubernetes environment. When installing on OpenShift, you use the CSM Operator. You install the CSM from the OperatorHub within the RedHat Hybrid Cloud Console.

    Note: When implementing the PowerMax CSI driver, we chose Fibre Channel which is the most common protocol on the PowerMax platform. You can also use iSCSI or NVMeoF as protocols if preferred. Note, however, that some Red Hat dev or tech preview features do not support all protocols.

    CSM Operator

    Follow these steps to install the CSM Operator.

    Step 1

    Open the Operators -> OperatorHub from the left-hand menu (see Figure 3) and in the right-hand screen, search for DELL. There should be two results, a certified CSM and community CSM. Click on the certified CSM.

    Figure 36.    Step 1 – Dell CSM Operator

    Step 2

    From the Dell CSM inset in Figure 37, click Install.

    Figure 37.    Step 2 – Dell CSM Operator

    Step 3

    Review the installation details in Figure 38 and click Install again to finalize.

    Figure 38.    Step 3 – Dell CSM Operator

     When complete, the UI will display the result as below.

    Figure 39.    Complete Dell CSM Operator

    After a successful installation, proceed with the CSI installation.

    CSI installation

    Dell provides documentation on the installation of the PowerMax CSI driver which you can locate at this link. This documentation may vary based on the CSM version. As of this writing, the current version is 1.15.1. Since this paper uses the basic functionality of the CSI driver and no CSM modules, we include the steps below for ease of reference; however, always refer to the official documentation if you encounter any issues.

    Reverse Proxy

    Unlike the other Dell CSI drivers, the PowerMax requires a Reverse Proxy. The function of the proxy is to regulate the REST API calls sent to the Unisphere instance. It can queue these requests to enhance the performance of the driver.

    Step 1

    Install the certificate manager:

    kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.16.1/cert-manager.yaml

    Step 2

    Create an SSL certificate and private key. You will supply this later in the installation when creating a TLS secret.

    Generate a configuration file (e.g., openssl.cnf). Here is an example. You can use this without modification if you wish.

    [ req ]

    default_bits       = 2048

    distinguished_name = req_distinguished_name

    req_extensions     = req_ext

    prompt             = no

    [ req_distinguished_name ]

    C  = XX

    L  = Default City

    O  = Default Company Ltd

    [ req_ext ]

    subjectAltName = @alt_names

    [ alt_names ]

    DNS.1 = "csipowermax-reverseproxy"

    IP.1 = "0.0.0.0"

    On a Linux host with openssl, generate the certificate and private key. Be sure to note the location as you will use them in a later step.

    openssl genrsa -out tls.key 2048

    openssl req -new -key tls.key -out tls.csr -config openssl.cnf

    openssl x509 -req -in tls.csr -signkey tls.key -out tls.crt -days 3650 -extensions req_ext -extfile openssl.cnf

    Fibre channel MPIO

    The following section discusses configuring MPIO on your OpenShift cluster.

    Zoning

    Complete zoning of the hosts to the array according to the best practices in the section FC connectivity. It is important to validate that the initiators are on the fabric and logged into the array, but not to create any host groups. The CSI driver creates the host groups through the REST API and if they exist, the installation will fail.

    MPIO

    You configure the DM-MPIO service on the OpenShift nodes through a machine configuration.

    Step 1

    Create a multipath.conf file using this as an example:

    cat <<EOF> multipath.conf

      defaults {

        polling_interval 5

        checker_timeout 15

        disable_changed_wwids yes

        find_multipaths no

      }

      devices {

        device {

          vendor                   DellEMC

          product                  PowerMax

          detect_prio              "yes"

          path_selector            "service-time 0"

          path_grouping_policy     "group_by_prio"

          path_checker             tur

          failback                 immediate

          fast_io_fail_tmo         5

          no_path_retry            3

          rr_min_io_rq             1

          max_sectors_kb           1024

          dev_loss_tmo             10

        }

      } 

    EOF

    Save the file locally, or where you normally run your oc/kubectl commands.

    Step 2

    Create a machine configuration file which will modify the DM-MPIO service. Here is an example file named 99-workers-multipath-conf.yaml. Be sure you place the multipath.conf file in the directory where you run this or it will be unable to convert the values.

    cat <<EOF> 99-workers-multipath-conf.yaml

    apiVersion: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/v1

    kind: MachineConfig

    metadata:

      name: 99-workers-multipath-conf

      labels:

        machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role: worker

    spec:

      config:

        ignition:

          version: 3.4.0

        storage:

          files:

          - contents:

              source: data:text/plain;charset=utf-8;base64,$(cat multipath.conf | base64 -w0)

              verification: {}

            filesystem: root

            mode: 400

            path: /etc/multipath.conf  

    EOF

    Apply the file:

    oc apply -f 99-workers-multipath-conf.yaml

    Step 3

    Lastly, enable the DM-MPIO service.

    cat << EOF > 99-workers-enable-multipathd.yaml

    apiVersion: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/v1

    kind: MachineConfig

    metadata:

      name: 99-workers-enable-multipathd.yaml

      labels:

        machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role: worker

    spec:

      config:

        ignition:

          version: 3.4.0 

        systemd:

          units:

          - name: "multipathd.service"

            enabled: true

    EOF

    Apply the file:

    oc apply -f 99-workers-enable-multipathd.yaml

    CSI driver installation

    Step 1

    Create a namespace for the driver:

    oc create namespace powermax

    Step 2

    Create the PowerMax credentials. In this file you specify the array, Unisphere for PowerMax environment for endpoints and management servers, and supply the username and password. In our environment we have two PowerMax arrays, so they are both listed. They share the same Unisphere environment.

    cat << EOF > config.yaml

    storageArrays:

      - storageArrayId: "000120001672"

        primaryEndpoint: https://172.16.105.200:8443

        backupEndpoint: https://172.16.105.201:8443

      - storageArrayId: "000120001473"

        primaryEndpoint: https://172.16.105.200:8443

        backupEndpoint: https://172.16.105.201:8443

    managementServers:

      - endpoint: https://172.16.105.200:8443

        username: smc

        password: smc

        skipCertificateValidation: true

      - endpoint: https://172.16.105.200:8443

        username: smc

        password: smc

        skipCertificateValidation: true

    EOF

    Create the secret with the following two commands:

    oc create secret generic powermax-creds --from-file=config=config.yaml -n powermax --dry-run=client -oyaml > secret-powermax-config.yaml

    oc apply -f secret-powermax-config.yaml

    Step 3

    Create the Reverse Proxy secret using the file you generated in the section Reverse Proxy.

    oc create secret -n powermax tls csirevproxy-tls-secret --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key

    Step 4

    The last step is to create the PowerMax custom resource. Below is a minimal configuration file which requires very few modifications in the envs section. If you plan on implementing any of the CSM modules, you need to use the detailed configuration sample file from the GitHub repository here. Dell recommends using the Installation Wizard to generate this file. Note that the variable X_CSI_REVPROXY_USE_SECRET must be set to true.

    apiVersion: storage.dell.com/v1

    kind: ContainerStorageModule

    metadata:

      name: powermax

      namespace: powermax

    spec:

      driver:

        csiDriverType: "powermax"

        configVersion: v2.15.1

        forceRemoveDriver: true

        common:

          envs:

            - name: "X_CSI_REVPROXY_USE_SECRET"

              value: "true"

            - name: X_CSI_MANAGED_ARRAYS

              value: "000120001672,000120001473"

            - name: X_CSI_POWERMAX_PORTGROUPS

              value: ""

            - name: X_CSI_TRANSPORT_PROTOCOL

              value: "FC"

          image: quay.io/dell/container-storage-modules/csi-powermax:v2.15.1

      # These are the modules which are optional and can be enabled by specifying to enable/disable.

      modules:

        - name: authorization

          # enable: Enable/Disable csm-authorization

          enabled: false

          # For Auth 2.0, use v2.2.0 as configVersion

          configVersion: v2.3.0

          components:

            - name: karavi-authorization-proxy

              envs:

                # proxyHost: hostname of the csm-authorization server

                - name: "PROXY_HOST"

                  value: "authorization-ingress-nginx-controller.authorization.svc.cluster.local"

        - name: resiliency

          enabled: false

        - name: replication

          enabled: false

        - name: observability

          # enabled: Enable/Disable observability

          enabled: false

          components:

            - name: otel-collector

              enabled: true

            - name: cert-manager

              # enabled: Enable/Disable cert-manager

              # Allowed values:

              #   true: enable deployment of cert-manager

              #   false: disable deployment of cert-manager only if it's already deployed

              # Default value: false

              enabled: false

            - name: metrics-powermax

              enabled: true 

    Save the file and create the resource.

    oc create -f powermax_resource.yaml

    Check if the CR is successful.

    ospmax170:~ # oc get csm powermax -n powermax

    NAME       CREATIONTIME   CSIDRIVERTYPE   CONFIGVERSION  STATE

    powermax   5m             powermax        v2.15.1        Succeeded

    You can also login to Unisphere for PowerMax and validate that there is a new host group for each OCP node in Figure 40. Note that if you scale your OCP, the resource will create a new host group for that node automatically.

    Figure 40.    CSI-created host groups

Prerequisites

  • You must meet the following prerequisites before implementing OCP with PowerMax.

    Server requirements for OCP are as follows:

    • A minimum of three Dell servers. For full feature functionality, they should possess an x86-64 architecture. You can utilize other architectures such as ARM, but it will limit some features.
    • 4 CPUs, 16 GB RAM, and 100 GB disk. Note the disk can be internal or SAN.
    • If you use only three servers, they will all be control-plane nodes and schedulable.

    Storage requirements for OCP are as follows:

    • An installed PowerMax 2500 or 8500 array with a PowerMaxOS version supported by the chosen PowerMax CSI release
    • At least four (4) front-end ports zoned to each OCP server, preferably in one-to-one zoning to two (2) dual-ported HBAs.

    Miscellaneous requirements:

    • A bastion server from which you can issue the kubectl or oc commands.
    • A DNS and NTP server.
    • OCP is a licensed solution. A default evaluation license is in place for 60 days.

Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform

  • Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform is an enterprise Kubernetes distribution that provides a consistent platform for deploying, managing, and scaling containerized applications across bare metal, virtualized, on-premise, and cloud environments. It extends upstream Kubernetes with additional components and automation to simplify cluster operations, application lifecycle management, and security.

    An OpenShift cluster consists of nodes, each running Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS (RHCOS), a minimal and hardened operating system derived from Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL). After initialization, each node uses the CRI-O container runtime to manage container images and execute workloads. The Kubelet agent registers the node with the control plane, reports node status, and handles workload scheduling instructions.

    OpenShift configures and manages cluster networking, ingress routing, and load balancing. It includes integrated services for monitoring, logging, and automated upgrades, enabling administrators to maintain cluster health and performance with minimal manual intervention.

    The platform provides an internal container image registry and access to a catalog of certified Red Hat and community operators and images, supporting a broad set of application services, including databases, runtimes, and developer tools. You can deploy applications using standard Kubernetes objects such as Deployments and StatefulSets, or managed with Operators, which encapsulate operational logic for installation, configuration, and lifecycle management.

    OpenShift supports building and managing custom container images from existing images and source code using integrated build tools. You can store these images in internal, private, or public registries and deployed through automated pipelines or direct configuration.

    Cluster architecture

    An OpenShift cluster is composed of two main node types: control plane nodes and worker nodes.

    • Control plane nodes host the core Kubernetes services that maintain cluster state and coordinate workloads. These include the API server, controller manager, scheduler, and etcd key-value store for persistent configuration data.
    • Worker nodes run user applications and services in containers. The Kubelet, CRI-O runtime, and SDN components operate on each worker to manage containers, networking, and storage.

    OpenShift adds infrastructure components such as the Ingress Controller, Cluster Network Operator, Machine Config Operator, and Authentication services, which integrate platform-level management and policy enforcement. These components ensure automated updates, configuration drift management, and consistent security posture across all nodes.

    Figure 1 shows a basic representation of the three-node, bare-metal OCP cluster as deployed in this paper which uses the Dell PowerMax as persistent storage.

    Figure 1.   OpenShift Container Platform bare-metal cluster

    Red Hat Hybrid Cloud Console

    The Red Hat Hybrid Cloud Console is Red Hat’s web-based interface for managing OpenShift clusters across different infrastructures — including bare metal, on-prem, and cloud environments.

    It provides centralized lifecycle management and visibility for clusters. Key functions are:

    • Cluster creation and installation: Launch clusters using methods like the Assisted Installer, installer-provisioned infrastructure (IPI), or bring-your-own (UPI).
    • Registration and inventory: View all clusters (connected or disconnected), their health, version, and status in one dashboard.
    • Lifecycle operations: Handle updates, scaling, and configuration changes.
    • Access management: Control cluster access through Red Hat organization and identity integrations.
    • Insights integration: Displays alerts, recommendations, and security information pulled from Red Hat Insights.
    • Subscription tracking: Shows OpenShift subscription usage, entitlements, and connected hosts.

    The console is the control plane for monitoring, provisioning, and maintaining multiple OpenShift environments.

    Figure 2.   Red Hat Hybrid Cloud Console

    OpenShift Web Console

    The Red Hat OpenShift Web Console is a browser-based management platform for Kubernetes clusters. You access it from within the Hybrid Cloud Console for individual clusters. It provides administrators and developers with a centralized dashboard to monitor cluster health, manage workloads, configure networking, and deploy applications. The console includes navigation options such as Projects, Workloads, Operators, and Virtualization, enabling streamlined access to cluster resources and operational tools. Key features include guided documentation for cluster setup, integration with identity providers, and support for advanced capabilities like OpenShift Virtualization and AI-driven enhancements. This interface is essential for maintaining cluster stability, observing real-time status indicators, and performing administrative tasks through an intuitive graphical environment.

    Figure 3.   OpenShift Web Console

Scaling

  • OCP cluster expansion is straightforward. The process to add a node mirrors the installation, allowing you to scale workers to handle increased VM and containerized workloads. Since adding nodes to OCP clusters is a common occurrence, we cover it here for completeness of deployment.

    Step 1

    Login to the Red Hat Hybrid Cloud Console. In the left-hand menu (see Figure 7), navigate to Cluster Management -> Cluster List -> <cluster_name>, ospcluster here. In the right-hand panel, click on the Add Hosts tab, and then the Add hosts button.

    Figure 25.    Step 1 – Add OCP host

    Step 2

    Choose your CPU architecture and the type of networking using the radio buttons below. Click Next.

    Figure 26.    Step 2 – Add OCP host

    Step 3a Static network configurations: Network-wide configurations

    In step 3 add the network information. This step is two parts, the network-wide (same as existing cluster) and the host specific. Start by selecting either the Form or YAML view. As the callout notes, use YAML if you are doing something more advanced with your node. For an example, we will use Form. Enter in the networking details, mirroring your original deployment of OCP. Click Next when done.

    Figure 27.    Step 3a – Add OCP host

    Step 3b Static network configurations: Host-specific configurations

    Next, enter the host specific information. This includes the MAC addresses (two for bonding) and the host IP. You can also add more hosts here if desired. Click Next to continue.

    Figure 28.    Step 3b – Add OCP host

    Step 4

    Begin by selecting a Provisioning type. Dell recommends using a minimal image file. Provide the SSH public key currently in use for the other nodes and then click on Generate Discovery ISO.

    Figure 29.    Step 4 – Add OCP host

    Step 5

    Finally, click on Download Discover ISO to pull the ISO through the browser. Alternatively, the wizard offers a direct URL or wget access.

    Figure 30.    Step 5 – Add OCP host

    Step 6

    Using the downloaded ISO, mount it to your chosen host and boot to it. As with the original cluster installation, it is non-interactive. You simply need to watch the Add Hosts screen for the new host to appear. If you receive a validation error as in Figure 31, review and resolve. Here, we had to configure NTP. Wait for the clocks to sync, at which point the validation error will disappear. Note that unlike the Insufficient status in Figure 20, if you are just missing an NTP server it will let you continue. Dell does not recommend doing this, however. Click the Install ready hosts button.

    Figure 31.    Step 6 – Add OCP host

    Step 7

    The installation does not take long to complete; however, even though the status will return as Installed, you may have to wait for the final reboot before the last step. Click on the View cluster events button to see when the reboot began. Until the system is up again, the cluster will not issue signing requests.

    Figure 32.    Step 7 – Add OCP host

    Step 8

    Finally, open the cluster console. Navigate to Compute -> Nodes in the left-hand menu. In the right-hand panel you will see the existing nodes. When the reboot completes on the new node, it will appear in the list. Initially the console will show the state as Discovered. Below the state will be the message: Approval required. In order to join the node to the existing cluster, it issues certificate signing requests, csrs. There are two requests it will issue. First, on discovery, and then to make the node Ready. Once you approve the first CSR, the node will be Not Ready. Approve the second CSR and wait for the node to come back as Ready. We include the steps in Figure 33. Note that you can also use CLI to view and approve the CSRs:

    • oc get csr
    • oc adm certificate approve <certificate>

    Figure 33.    Step 8 – Add OCP host

    The three node cluster is now a four node cluster and ready for additional workloads.

    Figure 34.    Updated four node cluster

Snapshots

  • OpenShift offers VM-level snaps which are storage array snapshots driven through the CSI driver utilizing TimeFinder/SnapVX on the Dell PowerMax.

    TimeFinder/SnapVX

    TimeFinder/SnapVX, or SnapVX, is a local replication solution that creates point-in-time copies, or snapshots, of PowerMax devices. SnapVX creates snapshots by storing changed tracks (deltas) directly in the SRP of the source volume. With SnapVX, you do not need to specify a target volume and source/target pairs when you create a snapshot. If the application ever needs to use the point-in-time data, you can create links from the snapshot to one or more target volumes. If there are multiple snapshots and the application needs to find a particular point-in-time copy for host access, you can link and relink until the correct snapshot is located. Snapshots are crash-consistent copies of the data.

    VM snapshot

    You can execute a snapshot from a number of places in the UI or use the CLI. In Figure 51 you can use the Actions menu and select Take snapshot or use the hyperlink in the bottom right-hand corner.

    The CSI driver acts as a bridge between the Kubernetes cluster and the storage array. When you create a VolumeSnapshot, the CSI driver sends a request to the storage array to create a snapshot of the PV. The storage array then creates the snapshot and returns a unique identifier to the CSI driver, which stores this identifier in the Kubernetes VolumeSnapshot object.

    You can query the snapshot through CLI or Unisphere for PowerMax. You can reconcile the two by viewing the SNAPSHOTCONTENT field in CLI and matching it against the snapshot name in the UI.

    Figure 52.    VM snapshot reconciliation in CLI and UI

Solutions Enabler

  • Solutions Enabler (SE) is a powerful command-line interface (CLI) tool designed for managing, automating, and monitoring Dell PowerMax storage systems. It provides granular control over a wide range of storage operations, including those that are unavailable in Unisphere for PowerMax. SE is especially well-suited for advanced users who require scriptable, reliable, and automation-friendly interfaces for enterprise-scale storage environments. Administrators can use SE to provision storage, manage replication (including SRDF and SnapVX), configure access control via masking views, and pull real-time performance and health metrics.

    Installed on a Windows, Linux, or UNIX management host, SE can communicate with arrays using either in-band (via HBA) or out-of-band (over IP) connections. It is frequently used in automated workflows, batch jobs, and integrations with orchestration platforms such as Ansible.

Summary

  • Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform is a powerful solution for modernizing application infrastructure, offering scalability, security, and flexibility across hybrid environments. The Dell PowerMax storage system complements this by delivering superior performance and advanced features such as local and remote replication for backup and disaster recovery. When integrated with OpenShift, PowerMax enables a highly resilient and scalable environment capable of supporting the most demanding workloads.

    This paper not only outlines the configuration steps for deploying OpenShift on Dell servers with PowerMax storage but also provides practical examples, including deploying containerized applications and virtual machines, as well as migrating workloads from VMware to OpenShift. By following these guidelines, organizations can accelerate adoption, reduce migration time through Red Hat’s copy offload technology, and ensure a successful implementation of OpenShift on PowerMax infrastructure.

Terminology

  • The following table provides definitions for some of the terms in this document.

    Table 1.      Terminology

    Term

    Definition

    Bootstrap

    A temporary host that runs minimal Kubernetes and deploys the OpenShift Container Platform control plane. In this paper, the installer automatically creates it on a node of the cluster.

    Containers

    Containers are lightweight, executable images that package software along with all its dependencies. By virtualizing the operating system, containers can run consistently across different environments.

    Control plane

    Manages the cluster, including scheduling, monitoring, and maintaining desired state.

    CRI-O

    CRI-O is an open-source container runtime specifically designed for Kubernetes. It provides a lightweight and stable environment for running containers and is fully compliant with the Container Runtime Interface (CRI) defined by Kubernetes.

    CSI

    Container Storage Interface is an API that allows Kubernetes to manage storage.

    CSR

    Certificate Signing Request

    Deployment

    A Kubernetes resource that maintains an application’s life cycle.

    FC

    Fibre Channel

    Kubectl

    The command line tool used with Kubernetes. For most commands, it is interchangeable with OC.

    Kubelet

    An agent that runs on each node and communicates with the control plane.

    Kubernetes

    Kubernetes is an open-source platform for automating the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications.

    MTV

    Migration Toolkit for Virtualization

    Namespace

    A way to divide cluster resources between multiple users or applications. It provides a logical partitioning of the cluster.

    NIC

    Network Interface Controllers

    Nodes

    The machines that run the workloads. Sometimes synonymous with hosts.

    OC

    OpenShift Client or oc is the command-line interface (CLI) for managing OpenShift clusters, including Kubernetes resources and OpenShift-specific extensions like projects, routes, builds, and deployment configs.

    OCP

    Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform

    Operator

    A method of packaging, deploying, and managing a Kubernetes application in an OpenShift Container Platform cluster.

    Pods

    The smallest deployable unit, typically containing one or more containers.

    PV

    Persistent volume

    PVC

    Persistent volume claim

    RHCOS

    Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS is the OS on the OCP nodes.

    VM

    Virtual Machine

    Worker node

    Nodes that run containerized applications. Also referred to as compute nodes.
