Troubleshooting

  • The following sections provide troubleshooting information for common problems encountered in OpenShift Container Platform (OCP). Review these steps before contacting support.

    Installation disks

    After Step 4 Host discovery, the Assisted Installer will display the storage options. If you are using a basic Dell server configuration, there are typically two disks which may or may not use RAID. If you see a considerable number of disks listed, however, it is likely the host sees mapped volumes from external storage. In addition, you may see a warning about multipath. In Figure 84, both of these are the case. There are seventeen devices for each host and two of the hosts use multipath.

    Figure 84.    Too many disks

    In such circumstances, start by expanding one of the hosts using the greater than symbol (>). The installer lists these disks in Figure 85. Note that this initial subset is comprised of only PowerMax devices. The installer chose one of these PowerMax devices (sdg) for installation. Note the gray checkbox indicating you cannot change it. As this host is not booting to PowerMax, you would need to unmask these devices from the host so that only the local devices remain. This will ensure OCP installs in the correct location. 

    Figure 85.    Host disks

    After you unmask the device, you must restart the Assisted Installer. Red Hat cannot dynamically update the disks. When the installer returns to the storage step, the new list in Figure 86 only includes a single, small PowerMax placeholder device. The installer now correctly sets the local installation disk.

    Figure 86.    Post-unmasking

    Boot from SAN

    Conversely, if you install on a server that does not have an internal disk that is at least 100 GB, you will see an insufficient disk size error for the installation. In the section Scaling, we covered adding a host to an OCP cluster which is in this state. The internal boot disk is 16 GB and while that is sufficient for many operating systems, it is not for Red Hat’s CoreOS. Therefore, we configured the host to boot to the PowerMax instead, presenting a 200 GB device. The installer, in our example, recognizes eight paths to the device and recommends using the multipath device which you can see in Figure 87 as dm-0.

    Figure 87.    Boot disk insufficient for installation

    If you use Boot from SAN, be sure to follow the Dell documentation for configuring the server. It is beyond the scope of this paper. Booting from PowerMax does offer an advantage over a local disk install because you have access to the replication technologies of TimeFinder and SRDF for local and remote replication if so desired.

    DNS entries

    In Step 6 Networking of the installation you supply two IP addresses, one for Ingress and one for the API. OpenShift generates a number of hosts or aliases that must resolve to these IP addresses. For example, in this environment we used IP 172.16.105.160 and 161. Upon completion, OpenShift lists the following:

    172.16.105.160       

    api.ospcluster.openshift.pmax.com

    172.16.105.161       

    oauth-openshift.apps.ospcluster.openshift.pmax.com

    172.16.105.161       

    console-openshift-console.apps.ospcluster.openshift.pmax.com

    172.16.105.161       

    grafana-openshift-monitoring.apps.ospcluster.openshift.pmax.com

    172.16.105.161       

    thanos-querier-openshift-monitoring.apps.ospcluster.openshift.pmax.com

    172.16.105.161       

    prometheus-k8s-openshift-monitoring.apps.ospcluster.openshift.pmax.com

    172.16.105.161       

    alertmanager-main-openshift-monitoring.apps.ospcluster.openshift.pmax.com

    There are two options for resolution: DNS or hosts file on your bastion server. Unless you always use the same host to access the OCP cluster, DNS is a better option to choose. We added our entries in PowerShell, though you can use a command prompt or the DNS Manager.

    PowerShell

    Import-Module DnsServer   # if needed

    Add-DnsServerResourceRecordA -Name "api.ospcluster" -ZoneName "openshift.pmax.com" -IPv4Address "172.16.105.160" -ComputerName "localhost"

    Add-DnsServerResourceRecordA -Name "*.apps.ospcluster" -ZoneName "openshift.pmax.com" -IPv4Address "172.16.105.161" -ComputerName "localhost"

    Test an address for resolution.

    PS C:\Users\Administrator> nslookup prometheus-k8s-openshift-monitoring.apps.ospcluster.openshift.pmax.com

    Server:  UnKnown

    Address:  172.16.105.44

    Name:    prometheus-k8s-openshift-monitoring.apps.ospcluster.openshift.pmax.com

    Address:  172.16.105.161

    PS C:\Users\Administrator>

    Adding a VM bridged network

    If you wish to configure a free NIC on your OCP nodes for use as VM network, you can use a MachineConfig file similar to the following for that purpose. Note that there are placeholder UUIDs in both source data. Be sure to update appropriately.

    apiVersion: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/v1

    kind: MachineConfig

    metadata:

      # The label specifies which machine config pool (MCP) this config applies to.

      # Change 'worker' to 'master' if you need it on control plane nodes.

      labels:

        machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role: worker

      name: 20-worker-bridge-eno3

    spec:

      # The configuration uses Ignition files to place NetworkManager connection profiles.

      # Ignition base64-encodes the content of the target file.

      config:

        ignition:

          version: 3.2.0

          # The 'files' array contains the two NetworkManager configuration files.

          files:

            # --------------------------------------------------------

            # Bridge Master Connection (br-eno3)

            # --------------------------------------------------------

            - path: /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/br-eno3.nmconnection

              mode: 0600

              overwrite: true

              contents:

                source: data:text/plain;charset=utf-8;base64,W2Nvbm5lY3Rpb25dCmlkPWJyLWVubzMKdXVpZD1kNjFhN2I4ZS0xNzNmLTQyN2YtOTRhMC01NjI3NTFmOTJjMzAKdHlwZT1icmlkZ2UKaW50ZXJmYWNlLW5hbWU9YnItZW5vMwphdXRvY29ubmVjdD10cnVlCgpbYnJpZGdlXQoKW2lwdjRdCm1ldGhvZD1kaXNhYmxlZAoKW2lwdjZdCm1ldGhvZD1pZ25vcmUK

            # --------------------------------------------------------

            # Ethernet Slave Connection (eno3)

            # --------------------------------------------------------

            - path: /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/bridge-slave-eno3.nmconnection

              mode: 0600

              overwrite: true

              contents:

                source: data:text/plain;charset=utf-8;base64,W2Nvbm5lY3Rpb25dCmlkPWJyaWRnZS1zbGF2ZS1lbm8zCnV1aWQ9YTNjNGY3YzgtNGQ1ZS00YjZmLTkwYTEtMmIzYzRkNWU2ZjdhCnR5cGU9ZXRoZXJuZXQKaW50ZXJmYWNlLW5hbWU9ZW5vMwptYXN0ZXI9YnItZW5vMwpzbGF2ZS10eXBlPWJyaWRnZQphdXRvY29ubmVjdD10cnVlCgpbZXRocnQdCgpbZGVmYXVsdF0KCm1ldGhvZD1kaXNhYmxlZAoKW2lwdjZdCm1ldGhvZD1pZ25vcmUK

    SSH node access

    If you forget to supply a public key during the installation process (Figure 15), you will be unable to SSH into your nodes. Under normal operating conditions, this is desirable; however, there are situations where it is necessary. For example, we detail in this paper how to use a free NIC for a VM network by enabling a bridge. We create the bridge through OS commands which require SSH access. It is possible, however, to create a MachineConfig file to authorize your bastion host to connect even after installation.

    Step 1

    Locate your public and private SSH key on the bastion host in the ~/.ssh directory. If the files do not exist, create them using ssh-keygen. Copy the contents of the public file.

    pshift105:~/.ssh # more id_ed25519.pub

    ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIAA0cejdmNJw9sBajBAzCxHeYqgNVOEZKSb4jREpMZcW openshift@baremetal

    Step 2

    Create two MachineConfig files, one for workers and one for master. If you have a simple three node cluster you do not require the worker file; however, if you add worker nodes in the future, creating both configurations will ensure new nodes get the key.

    Worker file

    Supply your public key under sshAuthorizedKeys.

    apiVersion: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/v1

    kind: MachineConfig

    metadata:

      name: 99-core-ssh-worker

      labels:

        machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role: worker

    spec:

      config:

        ignition:

          version: 3.2.0

        passwd:

          users:

            - name: core

              sshAuthorizedKeys:

                - ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIAA0cejdmNJw9sBajBAzCxHeYqgNVOEZKSb4jREpMZcW openshift@baremetal

    Master file

    apiVersion: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/v1

    kind: MachineConfig

    metadata:

      name: 99-core-ssh-master

      labels:

        machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role: master

    spec:

      config:

        ignition:

          version: 3.2.0

        passwd:

          users:

            - name: core

              sshAuthorizedKeys:

                - ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIAA0cejdmNJw9sBajBAzCxHeYqgNVOEZKSb4jREpMZcW openshift@baremetal

    Save both as YAMLs.

    Step 3

    Apply each file:

    oc apply -f 99-core-ssh-worker.yaml

    oc apply -f 99-core-ssh-master.yaml

    You can view the rollout by watching:

    cc get mcp -w

    The output will be similar to below. Once the UPDATED column is True, the job is complete.

    pshift105:~/.ssh # oc get mcp -w

    We edited the output below for readability. You can see the READYMACHINECOUNT move for the master move from 0 to 3 as each updates.

    NAME     CONFIG               UPDATED UPDATING  DEGRADED   MACHINECOUNT   READYMACHINECOUNT   UPDATEDMACHINECOUNT  

    master   rendered-master-xxx  False   True      False      3              0                   0                    

    worker   rendered-worker-xxx  True    False     False      1              1                   1                    

    master   rendered-master-xxx  False   True      False      3              1                   1                    

    master   rendered-master-xxx  False   True      False      3              1                   1                    

    master   rendered-master-xxx  False   True      False      3              2                   2                    

    master   rendered-master-xxx  False   True      False      3              2                   2                    

    master   rendered-master-xxx  True    False     False      3              3                   3           

    When the update completes, you can login to your OCP node. Note that Red Hat does produce a warning message about not using direct SSH access.

    pshift105:~/.ssh # ssh core@pshift101.powermax.os.com

    Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS 418.94.202505062142-0

      Part of OpenShift 4.18, RHCOS is a Kubernetes-native operating system

      managed by the Machine Config Operator (`clusteroperator/machine-config`).

    WARNING: Direct SSH access to machines is not recommended; instead,

    make configuration changes via `machineconfig` objects:

      https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.18/architecture/architecture-rhcos.html

    ---

    Last failed login: Fri Nov  7 15:19:42 UTC 2025 on tty1

    There were 4 failed login attempts since the last successful login.

    [systemd]

    Failed Units: 1

      NetworkManager-wait-online.service

    [core@pshift101 ~]$

Unisphere for PowerMax

  • Unisphere for PowerMax is an HTML5 web-based application that enables you to provision, operate and maintain PowerMax, VMAX All Flash, and VMAX storage systems.

    The most current Unisphere for PowerMax 10.3.0.x supports:

    • Storage systems (PowerMax 2500 and PowerMax 8500) running PowerMaxOS 10 (6079)
    • Storage systems (PowerMax 2000, PowerMax 8000, VMAX 250F, VMAX 450F, VMAX 850F, and VMAX 950F) running PowerMaxOS 5978
    • Storage systems (VMAX 100K, VMAX 200K, VMAX 400K, VMAX 250F, VMAX 450F, VMAX 850F, and VMAX 950F) running HYPERMAX OS 5977

    Unisphere for PowerMax also has a built-in Representational State Transfer (REST). The REST API allows you to access diagnostic, performance, and configuration data, as well as perform provisioning operations on the storage system through interfaces like the CSI driver. Full documentation for the Unisphere for PowerMax REST API is available at developer.dell.com or from the Help menu within the Unisphere for PowerMax User Interface.

Virtual Machines

  • You can use either CLI or the UI to deploy a VM. The UI also provides the ability to compose and execute a YAML directly. To create a VM using the UI follow these steps.

    Step 1

    In the left-hand menu of the UI (Figure 3), navigate to Virtualization -> VirtualMachines. In the right-hand panel use the drop-down menu for Create VirtualMachine and select From InstanceType.

    Figure 47.    Step 1 – VM creation

    Step 2

    In the upper left-hand corner of the panel in Figure 48, you can adjust the Project from the Default. Here we set the project to production-vms. Select a boot volume such as rhel8. OpenShift will clone this volume for the new VM. Note as we covered previously, these volumes reside on Dell PowerMax.

    Figure 48.    Step 2 – VM creation

    Step 3

    Scroll down the page and select an InstanceType that is either Red Hat or User provided. Here we select Red Hat provided General Purpose.

    Figure 49.    Step 3 – VM creation

    Step 4

    In the last section of the screen, make any adjustments to the VM such as Name or even Storage class. Since the creation clones the boot volume it does not have to retain the same storage characteristics. For example, the default powermax-fc-sc uses a Diamond service level, the most performant available. A boot volume does not require this level of performance so in this example we altered it to Bronze. Click Create VirtualMachine to complete the wizard.

    Figure 50.    Step 4 – VM creation

    Upon creation, OpenShift clones the image to a new volume with the Bronze service level.

    ospmax170:~/.kube # kubectl get pvc -n production-vms

    NAME                 STATUS VOLUME            CAPACITY       ACCESS MODES STORAGECLASS        

    rhel-8-ocp-vm-volume Bound  csivol-0c475fd7f7 30Gi      

    RWX          powermax-bronze-fc  

    ospmax170:~/.kube #

    OpenShift offers a VNC console via the browser.

    Figure 51.    VM detail and VNC access

VM Migration

  • In the following sections, we walk through migrating a virtual machine from VMware vSphere to OCP using MTV. This includes configuring the VMware vSphere provider.

    Provider

    Create a VMware vSphere provider.

    Step 1

    Login to the UI and navigate to Migration for Virtualization -> Providers in the left-hand menu. In the right-hand panel click the VMware box which is a link to a form.

    Figure 65.    Step 1 – VMware provider

    Step 2

    Fill out the mandatory information in Figure 66 as follows:

    • Choose a Project – it will default to openshift-mtv.
    • Provider type leave at VMware default.
    • Enter a Provider resource name.
    • Use the radio buttons to select an Endpoint type.
    • Enter the URL for the API endpoint.
    • Input the VDDK init image or use the VDDK init image archive to build a new one. Follow the hyperlink if necessary to learn how.
    • Dell recommends checking the box for VDDK async IO Optimization. This only impacts cold migrations.
    • Enter the Provider credentials for either ESXi or vCenter, depending on the endpoint.
    • Username
    • Password
    • Finally, either Skip certificate validation or supply the CA certificate.

    Click Create provider to complete.

    Figure 66.    Step 2 – VMware provider

    You can view the VMware provider source under Migration for Virtualization -> Providers. Upon creation of the provider, OpenShift inventories the vCenter or ESXi host. In Figure 67, the provider shows twenty-one VMs, seven networks, and two hosts in vcenter-2009. You can now migrate these VMs, provided they meet the necessary criteria.

    Figure 67.    Migration providers

    VM migration

    To migrate a VMware VM to your OpenShift cluster follow these steps. This is a cold migration which takes advantage of the async IO Optimization. Note that the vmdk disk type is not relevant. The migration copies the data, whether thin, thick, or zeroedthick.

    Step 1

    Login to the UI (Figure 65) and navigate to Migration for Virtualization -> Migration plans in the left-hand menu. In the right-hand panel click Create plan.

    Step 2

    In the next step input the following information.

    • Plan name
    • Plan project
    • Source provider (previously created)
    • Target provider (host or OCP)
    • Target project

    Click Next.

    Figure 68.    Step 2 – Migration plan

    Step 3

    The wizard now presents all the VMs from the source. Choose one or more VMs using the checkboxes. OpenShift will list any critical, warning, or information concerns for the VM. In the example in Figure 69, the wizard lists two warning concerns and one informational. The first warning is about CBT, which only impacts warm migrations. The second is self-explanatory about static IPs. Finally, the information warning simply states that the VMware feature DRS is not a feature on OpenShift. Click Next to continue.

    Figure 69.    Step 3 – Migration plan

    Step 4

    Next, you need to map the VM networks to the OCP cluster networks. In this example in Figure 70, we map the VM network to the default network. If you setup external networks, as covered in Adding a bridged network, you can choose that from the drop-down menu. You can name the network map or allow it to default as here. Click Next.

    Figure 70.    Step 4 – Migration plan

    Step 5

    In this step, map the VMFS datastore to a target storage class. If the VM vmdks reside in more than one datastore, you will need to provide a storage class for each mapping. In this example below, as we are doing a migration within the PowerMax array, we choose a storage class for the same array as the datastore. You can name the storage map or allow it to default as here Click Next.

    Figure 71.    Step 5 – Migration plan

    Step 6

    Select the migration type, cold or warm, and click Next.

    Figure 72.    Step 6 – Migration plan

    Step 7

    Complete one additional task by unchecking the box for Preserve static IPs because a cold migration does not support this. Click Skip to Review.

    Figure 73.    Step 7 – Migration plan

    Step 8

    Review the summary and click Create plan.

    Figure 74.    Step 8 – Migration plan

    When the migration plan is ready, you will see a Start box. Click to begin the migration.

    Figure 75.    Available migration plan

    Once the migration begins, you can follow the progress and various steps by clicking on the 1 VM hyperlink next to the Start button in Figure 75 and then expanding the arrow as in Figure 76.

    Figure 76.    Completed migration

    The time to complete a migration is dependent upon the data in the vmdks and the speed of the network. The size of the vmdks is not as relevant since if the disks are empty, they copy quickly. For example, this virtual machine’s 60 GB vmdk only contained 20 GB of written data and therefore copied quickly.

    PowerMax data reduction

    If you enable data reduction on the PowerMax array’s storage groups and run a VM migration with both the source and target volumes on the same array, you can expect full deduplication. If you use VMware as the source, remember that you only migrate the vmdks, not the datastore. Therefore, the source datastore volume will always have a little more storage allocation than the sum of the vmdks because of VMware VMFS metadata.
